title: Virtualizing the CPU: One Processor, Many Programs
topic: CPU virtualization — the OS gives each process the illusion of its own CPU by time-slicing one physical processor and performing context switches

beats.narration: Your laptop runs dozens of programs at once — but the chip inside has only a handful of cores. How can that be?

elements.content: How does one chip run a hundred things at once?

beats.narration: Picture four programs running side by side. Each one acts as if it owns the entire processor — its own counter, its own registers, its own little CPU.

elements.content: Four CPU cards in a row, each labelled A, B, C, D
Each card shows registers + PC, plus a pulsing 'running' dot
every program thinks it owns the whole machine

beats.narration: But underneath there is only one CPU. The operating system slices time into tiny pieces, and on each slice a different program gets to run.

elements.content: One large CPU box centred, labelled '1 CPU'
Horizontal time-slice strip below — coloured slots A B A C A D B A C A …
Sweeping playhead highlights the active slice

beats.narration: Between slices the OS saves the running program's state, and restores the next one's — a context switch, performed thousands of times every second.

elements.content: Process A state box on left (PC, SP, registers); arrow → memory
Process B state box on right; arrow ← memory
thousands of switches per second — so fast it feels parallel

beats.narration: One processor, many processes — that is the illusion the operating system calls CPU virtualization.

elements.content: One processor. Many processes. One illusion.
(this is what we mean by CPU virtualization)
